stem:
On the coronary care unit, a 58-year-old man with an acute coronary syndrome and poor renal function is started on a continuous intravenous heparin infusion (unfractionated), because he may need an urgent procedure and a short-acting agent is preferred. The nurse asks which blood result should guide changes to the infusion rate.

Which test is most appropriate?

options.A: Prothrombin time expressed as the INR
options.C: Plasma fibrinogen concentration by the Clauss method

correct_answer: D. Activated partial thromboplastin time ratio
why_correct: Unfractionated heparin potentiates antithrombin, mainly inhibiting thrombin and factor Xa, which prolongs the APTT. Its effect varies widely between patients, so an infusion is titrated against the APTT ratio, rechecked a few hours after each rate change. It is chosen here because it is short-acting, reversible with protamine and not dependent on renal clearance like low molecular weight heparin. Source: Heparin sodium Summary of Product Characteristics, eMC (MHRA-licensed), 2024.
why_wrong: A. The INR reflects the extrinsic pathway and is used to monitor warfarin, not heparin. B. Platelet aggregation studies assess platelet function, not the anticoagulant effect of heparin. C. Fibrinogen is relevant in DIC or massive haemorrhage, not in titrating heparin. E. D-dimer reflects fibrin breakdown and is used in assessing suspected thrombosis, not for dose adjustment.
pearl: Check the platelet count during heparin treatment: a fall of more than half, typically 5 to 10 days after starting, suggests heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, which is prothrombotic.
thinking: Intravenous unfractionated heparin infusion ↓ Effect is unpredictable between patients ↓ Prolongs the intrinsic pathway clotting time ↓ Titrate the rate against the APTT ratio ↓ INR is reserved for warfarin
exam_trap: A, Prothrombin time as the INR — it is the familiar anticoagulant monitoring test, but it is designed for warfarin and is a poor guide to heparin dosing.
takeaway: Unfractionated heparin infusions are titrated using the APTT ratio, whereas warfarin is monitored with the INR.

stem:
A retired builder aged 66 sees his GP after two chest infections this winter and a dull ache in his lower back for the last two months. A blood count shows a normocytic anaemia and his ESR is high. The GP wants to establish whether an abnormal monoclonal immunoglobulin is circulating in his blood.

Which test should be requested?

options.A: Plain radiograph of the lumbar spine

correct_answer: C. Serum protein electrophoresis
why_correct: Back pain, recurrent infection, anaemia and a high ESR in an older man raise the possibility of myeloma. Serum protein electrophoresis separates serum proteins and shows a discrete monoclonal band when a plasma cell clone is producing paraprotein. NICE advises sending it with a serum free light chain assay (or a urine Bence Jones test if free light chains are not available) for people aged 60 and over with persistent bone pain. Source: NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral, 2015 (amended 2025); NICE NG35 Myeloma, 2016.
why_wrong: A. A spinal radiograph may show bone lesions or collapse but cannot detect a paraprotein. B. Alkaline phosphatase is usually normal in myeloma because osteoblast activity is suppressed. D. An isotope bone scan often misses purely lytic myeloma lesions and does not detect paraprotein. E. CRP is a non-specific inflammatory marker and gives no information about monoclonal proteins.
pearl: Serum free light chains (or urine Bence Jones protein) can detect light-chain-only myeloma when serum electrophoresis looks normal.
thinking: Older man with bone pain and infections ↓ Anaemia and raised ESR ↓ Suspect a plasma cell disorder ↓ Need to detect a monoclonal band ↓ Serum protein electrophoresis
exam_trap: D, Isotope bone scan — it seems logical for bone pain, but myeloma lesions are lytic with little osteoblastic activity, so the scan is often normal and says nothing about paraprotein.
takeaway: Serum protein electrophoresis, with serum free light chains, is the key blood test to detect a paraprotein when myeloma is suspected.
notes: Reviewer fix: why_correct NICE sentence corrected: primary care sends SPEP with urine Bence Jones; lab adds serum free light chains Checker fix: the earlier 'reviewer fix' was out of date. NG12 (amended 2025) now recommends serum protein electrophoresis plus serum free light chains in primary care, with urine Bence Jones only if free light chain testing is unavailable. why_correct and pearl corrected.

stem:
A GP reviews blood results for a 71-year-old retired postman who had bloods taken for tiredness. His platelet count is 9 × 10⁹/L. When phoned, he says his gums have been bleeding when he eats and he has new purple bruises on his arms and a crop of tiny red spots on his ankles. He takes no anticoagulants.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Repeat the full blood count in two weeks
options.B: Reassure him that bleeding is unlikely while he feels well
options.C: Advise ibuprofen for his gum soreness and review next week
options.D: Send a routine referral letter to the haematology outpatient clinic
options.E: Arrange same-day hospital assessment for bleeding and its cause

correct_answer: E. Arrange same-day hospital assessment for bleeding and its cause
why_correct: A very low platelet count with spontaneous gum bleeding, bruising and petechiae means he is at real risk of serious haemorrhage. He needs same-day assessment to look for significant bleeding and to find the cause, such as immune thrombocytopenia, marrow failure or acute leukaemia, with urgent haematology input. Waiting or routine referral is unsafe. Source: NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral, 2015 (amended 2025); International consensus report on immune thrombocytopenia, 2019.
why_wrong: A. Delaying for two weeks ignores active bleeding with severe thrombocytopenia. B. He is already bleeding spontaneously, so reassurance is unsafe. C. NSAIDs impair platelet function and would increase his bleeding. D. A routine outpatient appointment is too slow for severe thrombocytopenia with bleeding.
pearl: In an older adult, new severe thrombocytopenia should not be assumed to be immune thrombocytopenia; a blood film and assessment for marrow disease are essential.
thinking: Very low platelet count ↓ Spontaneous gum bleeding, bruising and petechiae ↓ High risk of serious haemorrhage ↓ Cause unknown in an older man ↓ Same-day hospital assessment
exam_trap: D, Routine haematology referral — specialist input is right, but a routine appointment ignores the urgency of active bleeding with a severely low count.
takeaway: Severe thrombocytopenia with spontaneous bleeding needs same-day assessment, not watchful waiting.

stem:
Before a molar extraction, a 60-year-old man who had a coronary stent inserted two years ago tells the dentist that he bruises easily and that a recent shaving nick took a long time to stop bleeding. His GP checks a full blood count and clotting screen, which are both normal, including the platelet count.

Which of his regular medicines is most likely to be impairing his platelet function?
correct_answer: D. Aspirin
why_correct: Aspirin irreversibly acetylates platelet cyclooxygenase, blocking thromboxane A2 production and reducing platelet aggregation for the lifespan of the platelet. This causes easy bruising and prolonged bleeding from minor cuts despite a normal platelet count and normal clotting tests. After a stent, aspirin is usually continued, and UK dental guidance advises managing bleeding with local measures rather than stopping it. Source: SDCEP Management of Dental Patients Taking Anticoagulants or Antiplatelet Drugs, 2022.
why_wrong: A. Statins lower cholesterol and do not meaningfully impair platelet aggregation. B. ACE inhibitors affect the renin-angiotensin system, not platelets. C. Beta-blockers have no clinically relevant antiplatelet effect. E. Proton pump inhibitors reduce gastric acid and do not cause bleeding through platelet dysfunction.
pearl: Because aspirin's effect is irreversible, platelet function only recovers as new platelets are made, which takes about 7 to 10 days after stopping.
thinking: Easy bruising and prolonged bleeding from minor cuts ↓ Normal platelet count and clotting screen ↓ Suggests a platelet function defect ↓ Review drugs after coronary stenting ↓ Aspirin inhibits platelet cyclooxygenase
exam_trap: E, Lansoprazole — it is often co-prescribed with antiplatelets and may seem linked to bleeding, but it is gastroprotective and has no antiplatelet effect.
takeaway: Aspirin causes a bleeding tendency through irreversible platelet dysfunction even when platelet count and clotting tests are normal.

presentation: Bleeding with a normal platelet count
stem:
A dentist refers a 41-year-old man because the socket from a molar extraction kept oozing for two days. He recalls that small cuts take a long time to stop bleeding and that he developed a large haematoma after a hernia repair years ago. He takes no regular medicines. His full blood count, including the platelet count, is normal.

Which broad category of problem should be investigated next?

options.D: A defect of platelet function or of a clotting factor
options.E: Iron deficiency from chronic blood loss

correct_answer: D. A defect of platelet function or of a clotting factor
why_correct: A lifelong pattern of excessive bleeding after surgery and dental work with a normal platelet count means the number of platelets is adequate, so the fault must lie in how platelets work or in the coagulation cascade. Examples include von Willebrand disease, inherited platelet function disorders and mild haemophilia. A clotting screen with APTT and PT, and von Willebrand studies, would be the next steps. Source: NHS, Von Willebrand disease and Haemophilia, 2024.
why_wrong: A. Immune thrombocytopenia lowers the platelet count, which is normal here. B. Marrow failure produces cytopenias, not a normal blood count. C. Thrombotic microangiopathy causes thrombocytopenia with red cell fragmentation, which is absent. E. Iron deficiency may follow chronic bleeding but does not cause a bleeding tendency.
pearl: A normal APTT and PT do not exclude a bleeding disorder; von Willebrand disease and platelet function defects can have normal routine clotting tests.
thinking: Prolonged bleeding after dental extraction and surgery ↓ Lifelong pattern ↓ Normal platelet count ↓ Problem is platelet function or coagulation factors ↓ Investigate with clotting screen and von Willebrand studies
exam_trap: A, Immune-mediated platelet destruction — immune thrombocytopenia is the commonest acquired bleeding disorder, but it always lowers the platelet count, which is normal here.
takeaway: Excessive bleeding with a normal platelet count points to a platelet function or clotting factor disorder.

stem:
A 9-year-old boy who has moved to the area is reviewed in a paediatric haemophilia clinic. Specialist assays from his previous hospital show normal factor VIII and von Willebrand factor levels, but factor IX activity is markedly reduced. His mother's brother has the same lifelong condition.

What is his diagnosis?
correct_answer: D. Haemophilia B
why_correct: Haemophilia B, also called Christmas disease, is an X-linked recessive deficiency of factor IX. Like haemophilia A, it affects males, is carried by females and causes deep muscle and joint bleeds with a prolonged APTT. The specific factor assay showing low factor IX with normal factor VIII makes the diagnosis. Source: NHS, Haemophilia, 2024.
why_wrong: A. Haemophilia A is due to factor VIII deficiency, which is normal here. B. Von Willebrand factor levels are normal. C. Immune thrombocytopenia lowers the platelet count and is not an inherited factor deficiency. E. Factor XI deficiency is autosomal and would show low factor XI, not factor IX.
pearl: Haemophilia B is treated with recombinant factor IX; desmopressin is not useful because it raises factor VIII and von Willebrand factor, not factor IX.
thinking: Inherited bleeding disorder in a boy ↓ Affected maternal uncle suggests X-linked inheritance ↓ Factor VIII and von Willebrand factor normal ↓ Factor IX activity low ↓ Haemophilia B
exam_trap: A, Haemophilia A — it is the more common and familiar haemophilia with the same inheritance and clinical picture, but it is caused by factor VIII deficiency, not factor IX.
takeaway: Factor IX deficiency is haemophilia B, whereas factor VIII deficiency is haemophilia A.

stem:
A 34-year-old motorcyclist is admitted after a collision in which a deep thigh laceration bled heavily at the scene. He was previously fit and well, with no chronic illness. After surgical control of the bleeding and intravenous fluid resuscitation, his haemoglobin on the following morning has fallen well below his normal level.

Which red cell picture is most likely on that sample?

options.C: Anaemia with ring sideroblasts in the marrow
options.D: Anaemia with spherocytes and a raised bilirubin

correct_answer: E. Normocytic, normochromic anaemia
why_correct: In acute haemorrhage, whole blood is lost, so the remaining red cells are normal in size and haemoglobin content. Once fluid shifts and resuscitation dilute the circulating volume, the haemoglobin falls, revealing a normocytic, normochromic anaemia. Iron stores are not yet depleted, so microcytosis has not had time to develop. Source: Normocytic anaemia primary care pathway, Humber and North Yorkshire NHS, 2023.
why_wrong: A. Microcytosis develops only after iron stores are exhausted by chronic or repeated blood loss. B. Hypersegmented neutrophils with macrocytosis indicate B12 or folate deficiency. C. Ring sideroblasts reflect a disorder of haem synthesis, not haemorrhage. D. Spherocytes with raised bilirubin indicate haemolysis rather than blood loss.
pearl: The haemoglobin can be near normal immediately after acute bleeding because plasma and cells are lost together; it falls as volume is restored, so a single early value underestimates blood loss.
thinking: Acute heavy bleeding in a previously fit man ↓ Whole blood lost, cells unchanged in size ↓ Fluids and plasma shift dilute the haemoglobin ↓ Iron stores still intact ↓ Normocytic, normochromic anaemia
exam_trap: A, Microcytic hypochromic anaemia — blood loss is strongly linked with iron deficiency, but that picture needs chronic loss to deplete iron stores, which has not happened after one acute bleed.
takeaway: Acute blood loss initially causes a normocytic anaemia; microcytosis follows only with chronic loss and iron depletion.
notes: Checker: no national UK guideline states this textbook point directly; the source line names a regional NHS pathway that lists acute blood loss as a normocytic cause. Clinician may prefer a textbook citation.

stem:
A foundation doctor is taking a group and screen sample from a 77-year-old woman who needs red cells before hip fracture surgery. Her son watches the doctor label the tube at the bedside against her wristband and asks why so much care is taken over her blood group.

What is the main reason?

options.A: To prevent an ABO-incompatible transfusion causing acute haemolysis
options.B: To work out how many units she will need
options.C: To screen her blood for transmissible infections such as hepatitis B
options.D: To predict her risk of transfusion-associated circulatory overload
options.E: To detect allergy to donor plasma proteins

correct_answer: A. To prevent an ABO-incompatible transfusion causing acute haemolysis
why_correct: Recipients have naturally occurring anti-A and anti-B antibodies, so red cells of an incompatible ABO group are destroyed rapidly by intravascular haemolysis, which can cause shock, DIC, renal failure and death. Accurate grouping, careful sample labelling and bedside identity checks exist to stop the wrong blood reaching the wrong patient. SHOT reports repeatedly show that most such incidents arise from identification errors rather than laboratory faults. Source: BSH Guideline on the administration of blood components, 2017; SHOT.
why_wrong: B. The number of units depends on her haemoglobin, weight and clinical need, not her blood group. C. Infection screening is performed on donated blood, not on the recipient's group sample. D. Overload risk is judged from her heart and renal function and the transfusion rate. E. Allergy to plasma proteins is not detected by blood grouping.
pearl: A sample that is incorrectly labelled must be discarded and repeated rather than corrected by hand, because wrong-blood-in-tube errors can lead to ABO-incompatible transfusion.
thinking: Red cells needed before surgery ↓ Recipient has naturally occurring anti-A and anti-B antibodies ↓ Wrong group causes acute intravascular haemolysis ↓ Most errors arise from misidentification ↓ Careful grouping prevents ABO-incompatible transfusion
exam_trap: C, Screening for infections — infection risk is a well-known concern with transfusion, but donor blood is screened at the blood service, and the patient's group sample is not used for this.
takeaway: Careful blood grouping and identification exist to prevent ABO-incompatible transfusion and acute haemolysis.

stem:
Over the past month a 67-year-old man has felt exhausted, had a mouth ulcer that will not heal and been treated for a urine infection. He has also noticed purple spots on his shins. A full blood count taken by his GP yesterday shows anaemia, thrombocytopenia and a reduced neutrophil count. He is currently afebrile and haemodynamically stable.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Same-day assessment by the haematology team for suspected acute leukaemia
options.B: Start oral ferrous sulfate and repeat the blood count in four weeks
options.C: Repeat the full blood count in six weeks to allow recovery from a viral illness
options.D: Make a routine outpatient referral to the haematology clinic
options.E: Check haematinics and thyroid function and review with the results in two weeks

correct_answer: A. Same-day assessment by the haematology team for suspected acute leukaemia
why_correct: Fatigue, infections and purpura together with anaemia, thrombocytopenia and neutropenia suggest bone marrow failure, and acute leukaemia is the key concern. NICE advises a very urgent full blood count for these symptoms so that leukaemia is found quickly; once the count shows unexplained pancytopenia, patients can deteriorate within days from sepsis or bleeding. Same-day discussion with haematology allows an urgent blood film, further tests and treatment to start without delay. Source: NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral, 2015 (amended 2025).
why_wrong: B. Treating presumed iron deficiency ignores the neutropenia and thrombocytopenia and delays a serious diagnosis. C. Waiting six weeks is unsafe when symptomatic pancytopenia may reflect acute leukaemia. D. A routine referral is too slow for suspected acute leukaemia. E. Haematinics may be useful later, but a two-week wait is inappropriate when all three cell lines are low and he is symptomatic.
pearl: In suspected acute leukaemia, ask the laboratory to review a blood film urgently; circulating blasts confirm the need for immediate admission.
thinking: Symptoms of anaemia, infection and bleeding ↓ All three cell lines reduced ↓ Marrow failure suggests acute leukaemia ↓ Risk of rapid deterioration from sepsis or haemorrhage ↓ Immediate same-day haematology assessment
exam_trap: D, Routine haematology referral — it feels proportionate in a stable patient, but suspected acute leukaemia needs same-day specialist assessment rather than weeks on a waiting list.
takeaway: Symptomatic pancytopenia needs same-day haematology assessment, not a repeat test or routine referral.
notes: Checker fix: the draft said NG12 advises immediate specialist assessment for suspected acute leukaemia; in NG12 that recommendation applies to children and young people only (1.10.2). For adults NG12 gives a very urgent FBC (1.10.1); same-day haematology assessment for symptomatic pancytopenia is standard UK practice rather than an explicit NG12 recommendation. why_correct reworded. Key option shortened (was longest).

stem:
A 36-year-old man is admitted to the acute medical unit with a purpuric rash on both legs and blood-filled blisters inside his cheeks. His platelet count is 11 × 10⁹/L, while his haemoglobin and clotting screen are normal.

What is the principal immediate risk to him?

options.B: Venous thromboembolism related to immobility in hospital

correct_answer: A. Serious haemorrhage, including intracranial bleeding
why_correct: A platelet count this low, with wet purpura (blood blisters in the mouth), shows that primary haemostasis is failing. The main danger is spontaneous serious bleeding, such as gastrointestinal or intracranial haemorrhage. Assessment therefore centres on bleeding severity, looking for a cause and urgent haematology input. Source: International consensus report on immune thrombocytopenia, 2019; NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral, 2015 (amended 2025).
why_wrong: B. Clot formation is not the expected risk when platelets are severely reduced and clotting is normal. C. Tumour lysis follows treatment of a high-turnover malignancy and is not suggested here. D. Hyperkalaemia is not a feature of thrombocytopenia, although pseudohyperkalaemia occurs with very high counts. E. Hypercalcaemia is linked with malignancy such as myeloma, not with isolated thrombocytopenia.
pearl: Wet purpura (oral blood blisters) and retinal haemorrhages suggest a higher risk of serious bleeding than skin petechiae alone.
thinking: Very low platelet count ↓ Purpura with oral blood blisters ↓ Normal haemoglobin and clotting ↓ Primary haemostasis failing ↓ Main danger is serious spontaneous bleeding
exam_trap: B, Venous thromboembolism — he is an inpatient who might receive thromboprophylaxis, but the immediate threat from a profoundly low platelet count is bleeding, and anticoagulation would be dangerous.
takeaway: Severe thrombocytopenia with mucosal bleeding puts the patient at risk of life-threatening haemorrhage.
notes: Checker: kept in preference to PAN703 (intra-batch repeat, dropped). Distractors C-E (tumour lysis, hyperkalaemia, hypercalcaemia) are weak but unchanged from the source; B lengthened so the key is not longest.

stem:
A 47-year-old man on a haematology ward has severe thrombocytopenia after chemotherapy. His haemoglobin and coagulation tests are normal. The nurse looking after him asks which kind of bleeding she should watch for most closely.

Which pattern is most characteristic of a low platelet count?

options.A: Bleeding into large joints such as the knees
options.C: Skin and mucosal bleeding such as petechiae and gum bleeding
options.D: Bleeding that starts hours after a procedure despite initial control

correct_answer: C. Skin and mucosal bleeding such as petechiae and gum bleeding
why_correct: Platelets form the initial plug at sites of small vessel injury, so their deficiency shows up in the skin and mucous membranes. Typical signs are petechiae, purpura, nosebleeds, gum bleeding and heavy menstrual bleeding. In this man, with normal clotting factors, this superficial pattern is what to expect. Source: NHS, Haemophilia and Von Willebrand disease, 2024.
why_wrong: A. Haemarthrosis is typical of clotting factor deficiency such as haemophilia. B. Deep muscle bleeds also suggest a coagulation factor disorder. D. Delayed bleeding after initial control reflects failure of the fibrin clot, as in factor deficiencies. E. Retroperitoneal bleeding is more often associated with anticoagulants or factor deficiency than with low platelets.
pearl: Bleeding straight after a small cut points to a platelet or vascular problem; bleeding that starts later after initial control points to a coagulation factor problem.
thinking: Low platelets with normal clotting ↓ Platelets form the primary plug ↓ Small vessel bleeding in skin and mucosa ↓ Joint and muscle bleeds suggest factor deficiency ↓ Mucocutaneous bleeding is the platelet pattern
exam_trap: A, Bleeding into large joints — haemarthrosis is the classic picture of a bleeding disorder, but it belongs to clotting factor deficiencies rather than thrombocytopenia.
takeaway: Platelet disorders cause mucocutaneous bleeding; factor deficiencies cause deep joint and muscle bleeds.
notes: Checker: mirror image of PAN4798 (u74-g11, checked: haemophilia -> deep joint and muscle bleeds, contrasted with platelet disorders). Kept because the keyed fact differs, but the human reviewer should decide whether both mirror items are wanted.

presentation: Bruising with a normal platelet count
stem:
A 71-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation sees her practice nurse two weeks after starting a new tablet. She has several large bruises on her forearms and shins after only minor knocks. She has no nosebleeds or blood in her urine. Her full blood count, including platelets, is normal.

Which mechanism best explains her bruising?

options.A: Impaired coagulation caused by a drug effect
options.E: Excess platelet production in essential thrombocythaemia

correct_answer: A. Impaired coagulation caused by a drug effect
why_correct: A normal platelet count shows that the problem is not low platelet numbers. In a woman with atrial fibrillation who has just started a new tablet, the likeliest explanation is an anticoagulant impairing coagulation, and bruising is a recognised side effect. Her medicines should be reviewed and clotting tests and renal function checked where relevant. Source: NHS, Anticoagulant medicines: side effects, 2023.
why_wrong: B. Immune destruction of platelets would lower the platelet count. C. Bone marrow failure would cause cytopenias, not a normal blood count. D. Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, by definition, causes a falling platelet count and mainly thrombosis. E. Essential thrombocythaemia raises the platelet count, which is normal here.
pearl: Common drug causes of easy bruising include anticoagulants, antiplatelets, SSRIs and long-term corticosteroids.
thinking: Easy bruising ↓ Platelet count normal ↓ Thrombocytopenic causes excluded ↓ New tablet in a woman with atrial fibrillation ↓ Drug-induced impairment of coagulation
exam_trap: B, Immune-mediated destruction of platelets — bruising makes immune thrombocytopenia tempting, but it needs a low platelet count, and hers is normal.
takeaway: Bruising with a normal platelet count points to a coagulation or drug cause, so review the medicines first.

stem:
A 52-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department feverish, with gums that bleed on brushing and breathlessness on climbing stairs. Her blood count is low in every cell line. The on-call haematologist is asked to examine her peripheral smear.

What would she most expect to see if the cause is an acute leukaemia?
correct_answer: B. Circulating blast cells
why_correct: In acute leukaemia, immature blast cells replace the normal marrow, which causes the cytopenias, and they often spill into the blood. Finding blasts on the film in a patient with pancytopenia and fever strongly supports the diagnosis and needs immediate haematology referral. Bone marrow examination then confirms and classifies the leukaemia. Source: NHS, Acute myeloid leukaemia, 2023; NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral, 2015 (amended 2025).
why_wrong: A. Target cells suggest liver disease, thalassaemia or hyposplenism. C. Hypersegmented neutrophils suggest vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, which can cause pancytopenia but not blasts. D. Pencil cells are seen in iron deficiency. E. Spherocytes suggest hereditary spherocytosis or autoimmune haemolysis.
pearl: Auer rods within blasts on the film are characteristic of acute myeloid leukaemia.
thinking: Fever, bleeding and symptoms of anaemia ↓ All three cell lines reduced ↓ Concern for marrow infiltration ↓ Leukaemic blasts enter the blood ↓ Circulating blasts support acute leukaemia
exam_trap: C, Hypersegmented neutrophils — megaloblastic anaemia can also cause pancytopenia, but hypersegmented neutrophils point to B12 or folate deficiency, not leukaemia.
takeaway: Circulating blasts in a patient with pancytopenia strongly suggest acute leukaemia.

stem:
A 28-year-old woman with heavy periods has been started on oral iron by her GP for iron-deficiency anaemia. She asks which foods would add the most easily absorbed iron to her diet.

Which of the following is the best choice?
correct_answer: C. Lean beef
why_correct: Red meat contains haem iron, which is absorbed much more efficiently than the non-haem iron found in plant foods. Including lean beef, lamb or other red meat is therefore an effective way to increase her iron intake. Diet supports, but does not replace, oral iron in established deficiency. Source: NHS, Iron (vitamins and minerals), 2023.
why_wrong: A. Milk is low in iron, and its calcium can reduce iron absorption. B. White rice provides little iron. D. Butter contains almost no iron. E. Cucumber is mostly water and a poor source of iron.
pearl: Vitamin C taken with a meal increases the absorption of non-haem iron, while tea and coffee drunk with meals reduce it; UK advice is still to limit red and processed meat overall.
thinking: Iron-deficiency anaemia from menstrual loss ↓ Wants to increase dietary iron ↓ Haem iron is absorbed best ↓ Haem iron comes from meat ↓ Lean beef
exam_trap: A, Full-fat milk — it is seen as nutritious, but dairy is a poor source of iron and its calcium can reduce iron absorption.
takeaway: Red meat provides haem iron, the most readily absorbed dietary form.

stem:
On a haematology ward, a 60-year-old woman recovering from induction chemotherapy for leukaemia develops a high fever. She has no cough or urinary symptoms, her chest is clear and her line site looks clean, yet blood cultures later grow Pseudomonas.

Why are localising signs of infection often absent in this situation?

options.A: Too few neutrophils to mount a local inflammatory response
options.B: Infections in neutropenic patients are mainly viral rather than bacterial
options.C: Fever in neutropenia is usually caused by the drugs
options.D: Lymphocytes cannot migrate into infected tissue
options.E: Neutropenia itself causes fever without infection

correct_answer: A. Too few neutrophils to mount a local inflammatory response
why_correct: Neutrophils produce much of the local response to bacterial infection, including pus, swelling, redness and consolidation. When they are severely depleted, serious infection may cause only fever, without the usual localising signs. That is why fever alone in neutropenia is treated as sepsis, with empirical antibiotics given immediately, even when no source is found. Source: NICE CG151 Neutropenic sepsis, 2012.
why_wrong: B. Bacterial infections, especially Gram-negative ones, are the main early threat, and this patient grew Pseudomonas. C. Fever must be presumed to be infective, and drug fever is a diagnosis of exclusion. D. The problem is a lack of neutrophils, not failure of lymphocyte migration. E. Neutropenia does not cause fever on its own; fever implies infection until proven otherwise.
pearl: In neutropenia a chest X-ray may look clear despite pneumonia, and urine may contain few white cells despite a urinary tract infection.
thinking: Severe neutropenia after chemotherapy ↓ Fever with no focal symptoms or signs ↓ Bacteraemia confirmed ↓ Neutrophils drive local inflammation ↓ Few neutrophils, so signs are blunted
exam_trap: E, Neutropenia itself causes fever without infection — the lack of a source makes a non-infective explanation tempting, but this is unsafe, and the cultures here show genuine bacteraemia.
takeaway: Neutropenia blunts local inflammatory signs, so fever may be the only sign of serious infection.

presentation: Functional asplenia in sickle cell disease
stem:
The parents of a 4-year-old girl with sickle cell anaemia ask the paediatric nurse why their daughter must keep taking daily penicillin V and receive extra vaccinations against pneumococcus and meningococcus. They have been told any fever needs urgent hospital review.

What underlies her particular vulnerability to these organisms?

options.A: Low neutrophil numbers caused by sickling in the marrow
options.B: Iron deficiency impairing immune cell function
options.C: Antibody deficiency due to a failure of B-cell development
options.D: Kidney damage causing urinary loss of immunoglobulins
options.E: Loss of splenic function from repeated splenic infarction

correct_answer: E. Loss of splenic function from repeated splenic infarction
why_correct: Repeated sickling within the spleen causes infarction and fibrosis, so most children with sickle cell anaemia lose effective splenic function in early childhood. The spleen is key to clearing encapsulated bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type b and Neisseria meningitidis. This is why lifelong penicillin prophylaxis, extra vaccinations and urgent assessment of fever are advised. Source: UKHSA Green Book chapter 7, 2020; NHS, Sickle cell disease: treatment, 2022.
why_wrong: A. Neutrophil counts are usually normal or raised in sickle cell disease, not low. B. Iron deficiency is not the mechanism; many patients have iron loading from transfusion instead. C. B-cell development is normal; the defect is in splenic filtering and clearance of opsonised bacteria. D. Sickle nephropathy can occur but does not explain susceptibility to encapsulated organisms.
pearl: Splenic sequestration crisis, with a rapidly enlarging spleen and falling haemoglobin, is a separate early-childhood emergency in sickle cell disease.
thinking: Child with sickle cell anaemia ↓ Daily penicillin and extra vaccines ↓ Encapsulated bacteria are the threat ↓ Spleen clears these organisms ↓ Repeated infarction leaves functional asplenia
exam_trap: A, Low neutrophil numbers caused by sickling in the marrow — neutropenia is a familiar cause of infection risk, but the count is typically normal or high in sickle cell disease and would not single out encapsulated bacteria.
takeaway: Sickle cell disease causes functional asplenia, so encapsulated bacteria are a major threat and need prophylaxis.

stem:
On the haematology ward, a 52-year-old man with warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia has developed yellow sclerae. His urine is negative for bilirubin on dipstick testing, and his liver enzymes are normal.

Which type of bilirubin will make up most of the rise?

options.E: No rise; the yellow colour is due to carotenaemia

correct_answer: C. Unconjugated bilirubin
why_correct: Haemolysis increases haem breakdown, producing more bilirubin than the liver can conjugate, so the excess is mainly unconjugated. Unconjugated bilirubin is bound to albumin and not water-soluble, so it does not appear in the urine, which is why haemolytic jaundice is called acholuric. Normal liver enzymes support a pre-hepatic cause. Source: BCSH Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of hereditary spherocytosis, 2011 update; NHS, Jaundice, 2024.
why_wrong: A. A conjugated rise suggests hepatocellular disease or biliary obstruction. B. Direct bilirubin is essentially conjugated bilirubin, which is not the main fraction in haemolysis. D. Bile acids rise in cholestasis, not haemolysis. E. Carotenaemia spares the sclerae, whereas his sclerae are yellow.
pearl: Gilbert's syndrome also gives an isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, but with no signs of haemolysis.
thinking: Known haemolytic anaemia ↓ Yellow sclerae ↓ No bilirubin in urine and normal liver enzymes ↓ Pre-hepatic cause ↓ Mainly unconjugated bilirubin
exam_trap: A, Conjugated bilirubin — jaundice is often linked with liver disease, but conjugated bilirubin would also appear in the urine, which it does not here.
takeaway: Haemolysis causes a mainly unconjugated (acholuric) hyperbilirubinaemia.

stem:
A 9-year-old boy, whose mother has hereditary spherocytosis, is reviewed in the paediatric clinic. He is pale, mildly jaundiced and has a palpable spleen tip. His blood film shows spherocytes and polychromasia, and the direct antiglobulin test is negative.

How is his anaemia best classified?
correct_answer: C. Haemolytic anaemia
why_correct: In hereditary spherocytosis, abnormal membrane proteins make red cells spherical and fragile, and they are removed early by the spleen. This shortened red cell survival is a haemolytic anaemia, shown here by jaundice, splenomegaly and polychromasia from increased reticulocytes. A negative direct antiglobulin test helps separate it from autoimmune haemolysis. Source: BCSH Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of hereditary spherocytosis, 2011 update.
why_wrong: A. Megaloblastic anaemia results from B12 or folate deficiency and causes macrocytes, not spherocytes. B. Aplastic anaemia is marrow failure with pancytopenia and low reticulocytes. D. Iron deficiency causes small pale cells and no jaundice. E. There is no history of bleeding, and blood loss does not cause jaundice.
pearl: Parvovirus B19 can cause an aplastic crisis in hereditary spherocytosis, with a sudden fall in haemoglobin and very low reticulocytes.
thinking: Affected parent ↓ Pallor, jaundice, splenomegaly ↓ Spherocytes and polychromasia ↓ Shortened red cell survival ↓ Haemolytic anaemia
exam_trap: B, Aplastic anaemia — aplastic crises do occur in this condition, but polychromasia shows an active marrow, which is the opposite of aplasia.
takeaway: Hereditary spherocytosis causes an extravascular haemolytic anaemia.

stem:
A 66-year-old woman who had two units of red cells after a hip replacement a week ago returns to the orthopaedic ward from home. She reports tea-coloured urine, and the nurse notes that her eyes look yellow. Her haemoglobin is lower than it was after the transfusion.

Which complication should be suspected?
correct_answer: B. Delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction
why_correct: A delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction usually occurs days to a few weeks after transfusion, when previously formed red cell antibodies are boosted and destroy the transfused cells. Falling haemoglobin, jaundice and dark urine are typical. A direct antiglobulin test, haemolysis screen and repeat antibody screen are needed, and the transfusion laboratory should be told. Source: NHS England Clinical commissioning policy on delayed haemolytic transfusion reactions, 2020.
why_wrong: A. This causes breathlessness and pulmonary oedema during or soon after transfusion. C. This causes fever and rigors during or shortly after transfusion, without haemolysis. D. This causes acute respiratory distress within about six hours of transfusion. E. This is very rare in the UK and would not appear within a week or cause a falling haemoglobin.
pearl: Delayed haemolytic reactions are most likely in people previously sensitised by pregnancy or earlier transfusion; the antibody involved should be recorded to guide future transfusions.
thinking: Recent red cell transfusion ↓ A week later ↓ Jaundice and dark urine ↓ Haemoglobin falling ↓ Delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction
exam_trap: E, Transfusion-transmitted viral hepatitis — jaundice after a blood product suggests infection, but the timing is too short and the falling haemoglobin points to haemolysis.
takeaway: Jaundice, dark urine and a falling haemoglobin days after transfusion suggest a delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction.

presentation: Sickle cell disease presenting with painful crises
stem:
A 26-year-old woman who recently moved to the UK from Ghana registers with a GP. Since childhood she has had episodes of severe pain in her bones and joints, often after colds or cold weather, needing hospital care. Her bloods show a chronic anaemia with a raised reticulocyte count and bilirubin. Her brother had a stroke as a child.

Which condition is most likely?
correct_answer: C. Sickle cell disease
why_correct: Sickle cell disease is an inherited haemoglobin disorder in which HbS polymerises when deoxygenated, causing rigid red cells that block small vessels and are destroyed early. This explains recurrent painful vaso-occlusive crises, triggered by infection, cold and dehydration, alongside chronic haemolysis, and childhood stroke in a sibling is another recognised complication. Haemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC confirms the diagnosis. Source: NHS, Sickle cell disease, 2022.
why_wrong: A. This causes a low platelet count with bruising and bleeding, not painful crises or haemolysis. B. This causes pancytopenia with low reticulocytes. D. This causes microcytosis without haemolysis or bone pain episodes. E. This causes macrocytic anaemia and neurological features, not recurrent bone pain crises.
pearl: Hydroxycarbamide raises fetal haemoglobin and reduces the frequency of painful crises in sickle cell disease.
thinking: West African heritage ↓ Lifelong recurrent bone and joint pain episodes ↓ Triggered by cold and infection ↓ Chronic haemolysis with reticulocytosis ↓ Sickle cell disease
exam_trap: D, Iron deficiency anaemia — anaemia is common in young women, but iron deficiency does not cause haemolysis or recurrent pain crises.
takeaway: Recurrent pain crises plus chronic haemolytic anaemia suggest sickle cell disease.
